profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab between a faculty lead and a senior PhD student to organize a methodological survey paper tentatively titled "Explainable Deep Learning in Healthcare: A Methodological Survey from an Attribution View." The paper is intended for submission to a medical AI journal in six weeks, and the immediate agenda is to align on scope, literature collection workflow, section ownership, and what must exist by the end-of-month internal draft milestone. The expected outcome is a division of responsibilities for screening, taxonomy building, writing, and timeline checkpoints, while keeping the survey positioned as a practical reference for both AI researchers and clinicians.

members.name: Dr. Lena Zhou
members.expertise: Trustworthy machine learning, clinical prediction models, interpretability evaluation
members.background: Leads a university lab on reliable ML for healthcare and has published several papers on post-hoc explanation methods for EHR models; she routinely supervises survey and benchmark projects intended to seed larger grant proposals.
members.private_state: She wants the survey to sharpen the lab's methodological identity around rigorous attribution analysis in healthcare, stay narrow enough to finish on time, and produce an internal manuscript skeleton that senior collaborators can react to without the team overcommitting to a full systematic-review workflow.
hidden_assumptions: In this project, "attribution methods" primarily means techniques that assign importance scores to input features, time steps, tokens, or pixels for a fixed trained model, not the broader universe of explanation methods.

A paper counts as a healthcare paper for the survey only if its task and evaluation are clearly tied to real clinical use contexts or patient-derived datasets, rather than merely borrowing a medical benchmark as an example.
When a lab agrees on a "first draft," the expected deliverable is an internal manuscript scaffold with key sections, core tables, and representative citations, not a near-submission complete paper.
An initial literature screening pass should be lightweight and reversible because taxonomy boundaries usually shift once the first batch of papers has been seen.
Building from prior review work means inheriting the general framing and seed bibliography, then refining the team's own narrower scope rather than reproducing exhaustive review procedures.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Clinical NLP, literature synthesis, explainability for multimodal health models
members.background: A fifth-year PhD student who has worked on EHR and radiology-text models and previously helped compile evidence matrices for a fairness-in-healthcare survey; he is efficient at large-scale paper screening and structured comparison tables.
members.private_state: He wants this survey to become a substantial first-author paper with broad coverage that demonstrates command of the field, and he is trying to front-load extraction work so that later writing is faster and the manuscript looks comprehensive to external readers.
hidden_assumptions: In healthcare XAI practice, researchers use "attribution" broadly enough to include attention visualizations, concept-level relevance methods, and other explanation forms that localize model evidence, so excluding them would make the survey feel incomplete.
If a paper demonstrates on canonical healthcare datasets such as MIMIC, eICU, or CheXpert, it belongs in a healthcare survey even when the paper's main framing is methodological rather than clinical.
A promised "first draft" normally means most sections are already written in readable prose so coauthors can edit rather than react only to structure.
A good screening pass should capture coding fields immediately, because revisiting papers later is wasteful and creates inconsistencies in the evidence matrix.
Extending earlier review efforts means preserving their broad inclusion spirit unless someone explicitly narrows it.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an attribution method
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to organize the survey around an "attribution view" and to extract "attribution methods."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means feature-importance style methods that assign relevance scores to inputs or intermediate units for a fixed model, such as saliency maps, integrated gradients, occlusion, DeepLIFT, SHAP-style adaptations, and related variants.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader family of explanation approaches that indicate where model evidence comes from in practice, including attention visualizations, concept attribution, and some counterfactual or example-based methods when papers present them as attribution-like explanations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and professionally shared, and both members can mention overlapping examples like saliency and SHAP, so the boundary difference stays latent until paper inclusion or taxonomy coding happens later.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to cover "healthcare papers" and "healthcare applications" of attribution methods.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes papers grounded in real clinical prediction or decision-support settings using patient-derived data and clinically meaningful evaluation contexts, while excluding generic method papers that only happen to test on a medical benchmark or synthetic patient simulator.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes any explainability paper evaluated on well-known health datasets or healthcare-shaped synthetic data, because those papers influence how attribution methods are adopted and compared in the health ML literature.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share many familiar dataset names and both speak as if they are discussing the same literature neighborhood, so the disagreement is not about any single obvious paper but about a quiet boundary rule neither thinks needs stating.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the first draft milestone
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both commit to having a "first draft" by the end of the month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means an internal draft with the introduction framing, a stable taxonomy, a partially filled comparison table, and enough prose for coauthors to give directional feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means a mostly complete manuscript with all main sections written in coherent prose, with only polishing or discussion refinement left.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Academic teams commonly use "first draft" without defining completeness, and both interpretations sound reasonable and ambitious enough that neither participant perceives a need to calibrate the threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that Omar will "screen the papers this week" and use the lab's usual process.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a fast title-and-abstract triage with simple keep/maybe/exclude tags and only minimal notes, postponing detailed coding until the scope is settled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to combine screening with immediate full-text skim and structured extraction into a comparison matrix covering modality, task, attribution granularity, adaptation-to-healthcare details, and validation style.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both workflows are plausible under the label of screening, and the lab's "usual process" feels like shared shorthand even though each person is mentally compressing different amounts of work into that phrase.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to be a tight, finishable survey that reinforces the lab's niche on rigorous attribution analysis in healthcare, not a sprawling explainability catalog. Six weeks is short, so the end-of-month first draft should really be an internal manuscript scaffold: intro framing, stable section structure, a taxonomy figure, core comparison tables, and enough representative citations that the senior collaborators can react. If we keep saying an attribution view, that should naturally steer us toward feature-importance style methods on fixed trained models rather than every explanation family.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Omar. I want us to use this meeting to map a realistic six-week path for the survey. The title can still evolve, but the core idea is a methodological survey from an attribution view, grounded in healthcare applications, and I want us aligned on what has to happen between now and the end of the month so we can have a first draft ready to circulate internally.

turns.inner_thought: Great, this can become a serious first-author survey if I build the literature base broadly from the start. I already know a lot of the benchmark-heavy EHR, imaging, and multimodal explainability papers, and those absolutely belong in the healthcare paper pool. If I collect comprehensively now, the writing later can look authoritative rather than selective.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can start assembling the healthcare paper pool right away. I already have a pretty good mental map of the benchmark-heavy EHR and imaging explainability literature, plus some multimodal work, so I can pull together an initial set quickly and then expand from there.

turns.inner_thought: I should emphasize scope without sounding restrictive. The paper needs to stay centered on attribution methods in the narrower sense I use in my own work—importance assigned to inputs, timesteps, tokens, pixels, or related units for a fixed model. If we drift into the full interpretability landscape, we'll lose crispness and miss the deadline.
turns.utterance: Good. One thing I do want to be deliberate about is keeping the taxonomy centered on attribution methods. If we let it drift into the entire interpretability landscape, the survey will get fuzzy very fast. I'd rather the framing stay methodologically crisp and then make the healthcare angle do the work of broadening the relevance.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and in practice that umbrella should be broad enough to match what healthcare readers actually encounter: saliency, attention views, concept-level relevance, and adjacent attribution-like explanations. If we organize them together, the survey will feel complete and useful rather than artificially narrow.
turns.utterance: I agree. To make that concrete, I can set up a comparison sheet under the attribution umbrella so readers can see the landscape in one place. Grouping the main families that people are likely to encounter should make it easier for clinicians and ML readers to orient themselves without us losing the thread.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this week light. Screening should just be a quick, reversible title-and-abstract triage with maybe simple notes, not a full evidence extraction exercise. Taxonomy boundaries will shift after we see the first wave of papers, and I don't want the team locked into an overly elaborate matrix too early.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. For this week, though, let's keep the screening pass quick and use the lab's usual process. I mostly want an initial view of the paper set so we can tighten the categories after we've seen what is actually there, rather than over-engineering the structure up front.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—I can call it screening, but I'll fold in structured extraction while I'm there. It's inefficient to revisit papers later, and if I populate modality, task, attribution grouping, adaptation details, and validation style now, the evidence matrix will already be mostly built by the time we start drafting.
turns.utterance: Works for me. While I screen the papers this week, I'll also fill the main extraction columns so we have the backbone of the evidence matrix in place early. That way, when we move into writing, we're not starting from a blank table.

turns.inner_thought: I should gently signal the healthcare boundary. For me, healthcare papers should really be tied to clinical prediction or decision-support contexts with patient-derived data and meaningful clinical evaluation, even if the attribution method itself came from general ML. I don't want the survey dominated by generic method papers that merely borrow a medical benchmark.
turns.utterance: And on coverage, I especially want us to stay anchored in healthcare papers that connect to real clinical decision-support settings. I'm completely happy if the underlying attribution methods come from general-domain ML, but the healthcare applications should feel genuinely grounded.

turns.inner_thought: That's compatible with keeping the net broad. Papers on MIMIC, eICU, CheXpert, and even synthetic EHR benchmarks still shape how people understand attribution in healthcare, even when the paper is more methodological than clinical. I should make sure those are captured so the survey doesn't look parochial.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. I'll make sure the pool also captures method-oriented papers that are validated on datasets like MIMIC, eICU, CheXpert, and related benchmarks, because they still show how attribution is being used in healthcare applications and they often influence what people adopt.

turns.inner_thought: I should define the milestone in a way that keeps expectations manageable, but without making it sound less ambitious. By end of month, I need the introduction framing, a stable taxonomy figure, a seeded comparison table, and enough section prose that coauthors can give directional feedback. Not a polished near-submission manuscript.
turns.utterance: So just to make the milestone concrete, by the end-of-month first draft I mainly want the introduction framing in decent shape, the taxonomy figure stabilized, and the comparison table seeded enough that I can send the document to coauthors for reactions. If those pieces are coherent, we'll be in a very good place for the final stretch.

turns.inner_thought: I'll push for something much closer to a full manuscript. If I front-load the screening and extraction now, I can probably have most sections written in readable prose by then, which will make the paper look serious to everyone. I'll take ownership of the screening workflow and the section on healthcare-specific adaptations so the draft feels comprehensive.
turns.utterance: Got it. I'll aim for the first draft to be essentially complete apart from final polishing, and I'll take point on screening the papers this week plus drafting the section on healthcare-specific adaptations of attribution methods. Then we can use the last stretch to tighten the framing and resolve anything that needs a stronger synthesis.
